correctness.rationale: For all integers \(n\ge4\), radial weights \(1/2\le r\le1\), and \(p\ge0\), the exact zero-mass quadratic form splits into a global coefficient \(g_{n,r}(p)=(n-3)(2r)^p+2-2nr^p\) and rim-frequency eigenvalues \(-(2r)^p+2(1-(2r)^p)\cos(2\pi k/n)\). Their sharp signs yield two thresholds; the global coefficient strictly increases and crosses zero exactly once. Monotonicity in radial weight gives one crossover and a unique optimum, and Fourier multiplicities give the endpoint affine dimensions. Taylor expansions prove the sharp asymptotics. The executable `verify.py` passed 10,362 independently reconstructed finite metric, quadratic-form, spectrum, kernel, and asymptotic assertions. Finite checks are not substituted for the universal proof.

value.rationale: The theorem solves a natural geometric optimization problem: choosing one uniform radial edge length to maximize the Hilbert-snowflake exponent of a metric wheel. It classifies the entire parameter region, distinguishes global hub/rim and high-frequency rim obstructions, identifies endpoint dimension and parity, and proves a sharp \(2/n\) boundary layer. The four-rim optimum becomes a literal Euclidean square with its center. These are structural invariant results, not a one-off table or routine \(p=1\) restatement.
